cards.claim: Training throughput exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with batch size, peaking at an optimal value and then declining; this throughput ceiling is distinct from inference which monotonically improves with larger batch sizes.
cards.conditions: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet; edge CPU devices (Raspberry Pi 4, Jetson Xavier, Banana Pi, ZCU102); gradient-based training with backpropagation
cards.effect: Optimal batch size achieves ≥1.25× throughput improvement over maximum batch size (peaks ~2× on Raspberry Pi); throughput degrades beyond optimal point
cards.evidence: Empirical measurement across devices and datasets; comparison of training vs. inference throughput curves
cards.quote: a distinct pattern emerges across all edge devices where the training throughput peaks and subsequently declines as the batch size increases. This phenomenon represents a throughput ceiling, where hardware reaches its maximum processing rate for a given input batch size.

cards.claim: The throughput ceiling in training is caused by memory overhead from storing intermediate activations required for backpropagation, which scales with batch size. Inference lacks this constraint and thus does not exhibit a throughput ceiling.
cards.conditions: ResNet-18 training with gradient computation; backward pass dependency on intermediate layer activations
cards.effect: Training throughput begins declining when batch size exceeds memory-optimal point; inference throughput continues improving with larger batches
cards.evidence: Direct mechanistic explanation comparing training vs. inference computational graphs and memory requirements
cards.quote: The bottleneck is due to the need to store intermediate activations from the ResNet-18 layers required for the backward pass, which scales with the batch size. In contrast, inference does not require the retention of intermediate activations.

cards.claim: Optimal batch size for training requires pairing with linearly scaled learning rate to maintain accuracy; this accounts for the interdependence between batch size and learning rate hyperparameters.
cards.conditions: Continual learning with Experience Replay on CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet; mini-batch sizes tested: 2, 5, 7, 14, 16, 64, 256; base learning rate 0.03
cards.effect: Linear LR scaling preserves accuracy when using non-maximum batch size, preventing accuracy degradation
cards.evidence: Empirical validation across CL and SL paradigms with systematic LR scaling relative to batch size changes
cards.quote: In the CL paradigm, optimal learning performance was observed when the obtained batch size was paired with a linearly scaled learning rate, [...] This scaling was performed relative to the base learning rate configurations typically used in standard benchmarks.

cards.claim: Batch size tuning effectiveness differs between training and inference: training shows significant non-linearity with a distinct optimum, while inference monotonically improves and thus should default to maximum batch size.
cards.conditions: Gradient-based training vs. forward-pass-only inference on same hardware and model architecture
cards.effect: Training: ≥1.25× speedup at optimal vs. max batch size; Inference: negligible difference between optimal and max batch size
cards.evidence: Comparative throughput curves (Figures 2 and 3) across all tested edge platforms
cards.quote: Although batch size tuning can be applied to model inference, the data suggest that larger batch sizes generally yield higher throughput. [...] Thus, it can be concluded that for inference tasks, utilizing the maximum possible batch size is preferable, as the performance remains nearly identical to the baseline.
